Home News Arts and Culture Business Sports Opinion Research Live TV/Radio Media Elections Dark Mode Dark mode --> Opinion Ghana’s nuclear journey: From Nkrumah’s vision to a new investment commitment Source : Lom Nuku Ahlijah 17 November 2026 11:24pm ▶ Listen to this article Audio By Carbonatix
Ghana’s proposed US$200 million investment in nuclear power readiness marks a significant step in a journey that began more than six decades ago. It renews an ambition rooted in the country’s earliest development agenda: building the energy capacity to sustain industrialisation and economic transformation.
During a recent discussion in the media, I expressed support for this investment. Its importance becomes clearer when placed within the history of Ghana’s efforts to include nuclear power in its electricity generation mix.
In 1961, under President Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana decided to undertake the Ghana Nuclear Reactor Project. Its immediate purpose was to establish a research reactor for scientific research, training and radioisotope production. The longer objective was to develop the human resources and technical knowledge necessary for nuclear electricity generation.
The establishment of the Ghana Atomic Energy Commission gave that ambition an institutional foundation. Nuclear science formed part of a broader vision in which education, infrastructure and energy would support an industrial economy.
Nkrumah recognised that economic transformation required deliberate preparation for future electricity demand. Factories, mineral processing facilities and expanding cities would need dependable power. His overthrow in 1966 interrupted the early nuclear power agenda, although Ghana’s scientific work in nuclear technology continued.
An important milestone followed during President Jerry John Rawlings’ administration. The Ghana Research Reactor, GHARR-1, achieved first criticality in December 1994 and was formally commissioned in March 1995. It served research and training purposes, giving Ghanaian scientists practical experience in reactor operations and nuclear applications. That experience helped strengthen the country’s technical foundation for future development.
The modern policy drive towards nuclear electricity gained renewed momentum during the energy difficulties of the 2000s. In 2007, President John Agyekum Kufuor’s administration established a presidential committee chaired by Professor Daniel Adzei Bekoe to assess the potential role of nuclear power. Its recommendations informed Cabinet’s decision in 2008 to include nuclear energy in Ghana’s electricity generation mix.
Successive administrations continued the preparatory work. A major legal development came during President John Dramani Mahama’s first administration with the passage of the Nuclear Regulatory Authority Act, 2015, Act 895. The Act established an independent regulatory authority and provided a framework for licensing, inspection, enforcement and the protection of people and the environment from radiation risks.
This legal foundation is central to the credibility of Ghana’s ambitions. Nuclear power requires institutions capable of examining technical proposals, enforcing standards and holding operators accountable throughout the life of a facility. Regulatory competence must develop alongside the programme itself.
Ghana’s preparations also underwent international scrutiny. The International Atomic Energy Agency conducted an Integrated Nuclear Infrastructure Review in 2017 and a follow-up mission in 2019. In 2022, under President Nana Addo Dankwa Akufo-Addo, Ghana formally announced its transition into Phase Two of the programme, involving preparatory work towards construction following a policy decision.
This history reflects contributions by successive governments, scientists, engineers and public institutions. It demonstrates the value of continuity in national development. Projects requiring decades of preparation depend on administrations preserving institutional knowledge and advancing the work they inherit.
The latest commitment under President Mahama’s administration provides an opportunity to move that work forward with a defined funding proposal and timetable.
The 2027 Budget proposes US$200 million for a 24-month nuclear readiness programme, running from January 2027 to December 2028. The preparations include site studies, technology selection, environmental assessment, financing, licensing, safeguards, emergency planning and the safety case. The stated target is to complete readiness and sign an engineering, procurement, construction and financing contract for a fully state-owned nuclear power plant by December 2028.
The nature of this commitment must be communicated accurately. The US$200 million is intended for readiness activities. It represents preparatory expenditure rather than the full construction cost of a nuclear plant. The Budget also explicitly recognises that completing readiness in 2028 does not mean nuclear electricity generation will begin in that year.
That distinction should help establish realistic public expectations. The quality of preparation will influence the project’s eventual cost, safety, financing and delivery.
My support for this investment rests on the need to plan for Ghana’s future productive capacity. Our electricity policy must account for the demands of an economy seeking to manufacture more goods, process more of its natural resources and support increasingly sophisticated businesses.
Nuclear power deserves consideration within that long-term planning. Its suitability must be assessed alongside other generation sources, the capacity of the national grid, financing conditions and projected demand. The objective should be a dependable electricity system that supports competitive production.
There is also an opportunity to build Ghanaian skills and expand participation in a technically demanding industry. A nuclear programme can create work across engineering, construction, environmental management, law, finance, security and technical services. The extent to which Ghanaians benefit will depend on deliberate training, credible local participation requirements and opportunities for domestic businesses.
Training must therefore be connected to identifiable roles. Universities, technical institutions and professional bodies should be involved early enough to prepare people for the work the programme will require. Local participation must similarly be supported by standards, certification and supplier development.
As a lawyer and energy policy analyst, I consider governance fundamental to the success of this investment. Transparent procurement, rigorous technology assessment and financing terms that protect the public interest must guide implementation.
The regulator must have the resources, expertise and independence to make decisions on safety grounds. Communities must receive clear information and meaningful opportunities to participate. Waste management, emergency preparedness and eventual decommissioning must be incorporated into planning and financing from the outset.
These requirements give substance to the investment. Public confidence will grow through demonstrable competence, openness and accountability.
Ghana’s nuclear journey has endured interruptions, renewed commitments and years of institutional preparation. The proposed investment offers President Mahama’s administration an opportunity to advance this national undertaking through measurable progress.
The task now is to turn funding commitments into sound decisions, capable institutions and a credible route towards implementation. That is how an ambition first pursued in the early years of independence can contribute to Ghana’s next stage of development.
The writer is a lawyer, law lecturer, author and energy and public policy analyst.
